column2: In SQL Server, a common table expression (CTE) defines a {{c1::named result set}} from a query.
column3:
The name can serve as a table source in the following query, even though no separate table is created.
WITH N AS (
    SELECT 1 AS n
)
SELECT n FROM N;
Review source

column2: A SQL Server CTE definition is available to {{c1::one following statement}}.
column3:
Two references inside one SELECT are allowed. A second SELECT needs a new definition or a separately stored result.
WITH N AS (
    SELECT 1 AS n
)
SELECT n FROM N;
Review source

column2: {{c1::WITH}} N AS (SELECT 1 AS n) SELECT n FROM N; defines and uses a SQL Server CTE.
column3:
The parenthesized SELECT defines N. SELECT n FROM N consumes the definition immediately.
WITH N AS (
    SELECT 1 AS n
)
SELECT n FROM N;
Review source

column2: Before a SQL Server CTE, terminate the preceding statement in the same batch with {{c1::a semicolon}}.
column3:
The semicolon belongs to the statement before WITH. It is not part of the CTE name or definition.
SELECT 1 AS PreviousResult;
WITH N AS (SELECT 2 AS n)
SELECT n FROM N;
Review source

column2: Separate multiple SQL Server CTE definitions in one WITH clause with {{c1::commas}}.
column3:
The comma marks the boundary between two named queries. Do not start a second WITH at that boundary.
WITH Sales AS (SELECT 10 AS Amount),
     Totals AS (SELECT SUM(Amount) AS Total FROM Sales)
SELECT Total FROM Totals;
Review source

column2: A SQL Server CTE can reference a different CTE defined {{c1::earlier in the same WITH clause}}.
column3:
Order the definitions so a prerequisite appears before its consumer. Only recursion permits a definition to reference itself.
WITH Sales AS (SELECT 10 AS Amount),
     Totals AS (SELECT SUM(Amount) AS Total FROM Sales)
SELECT Total FROM Totals;
Review source

column2: To use one SQL Server CTE in both inputs of a self-join, assign its references {{c1::different aliases}}.
column3:
For example, alias one reference e and the other m when matching employees to managers.
WITH Employees AS (
    SELECT EmployeeID, ManagerID FROM dbo.Employees
)
SELECT e.EmployeeID, m.EmployeeID AS ManagerID
FROM Employees AS e
JOIN Employees AS m ON e.ManagerID = m.EmployeeID;
Review source

column2: In SQL Server, CTE results are {{c1::not materialized}} automatically for reuse.
column3:
Do not treat a CTE as a cache. Inspect the plan or store the result separately if repeated work matters.
Review source

column2: A SQL Server CTE that references itself to traverse a hierarchy is a {{c1::recursive CTE}}.
column3:
Each step takes rows from the last step and follows another level of the relationship.
WITH N AS (
    SELECT 1 AS n
    UNION ALL
    SELECT n + 1 FROM N WHERE n < 3
)
SELECT n FROM N
ORDER BY n;
Review source

column2: In a recursive SQL Server CTE, the {{c1::anchor member}} supplies the initial rows.
column3:
The anchor produces the root or other starting rows without using the recursive result.
WITH N AS (
    SELECT 1 AS n
    UNION ALL
    SELECT n + 1 FROM N WHERE n < 3
)
SELECT n FROM N
ORDER BY n;
Review source

column2: A SQL Server CTE's recursive member uses rows from {{c1::the immediately preceding iteration}}.
column3:
If the anchor returns a manager and the first step returns employees, the next step starts with those employees.
WITH N AS (
    SELECT 1 AS n
    UNION ALL
    SELECT n + 1 FROM N WHERE n < 3
)
SELECT n FROM N
ORDER BY n;
Review source

column2: In a SQL Server recursive CTE, {{c1::UNION ALL}} connects the last anchor member to the first recursive member.
column3:
The operator combines the anchor and recursive outputs without removing repeated rows.
WITH N AS (
    SELECT 1 AS n
    UNION ALL
    SELECT n + 1 FROM N WHERE n < 3
)
SELECT n FROM N
ORDER BY n;
Review source

column2: SQL Server CTE recursion normally stops when the recursive member {{c1::returns no rows}}.
column3:
An empty step leaves nothing for the next step to process. Make sure cycles cannot keep supplying rows.
WITH N AS (
    SELECT 1 AS n
    UNION ALL
    SELECT n + 1 FROM N WHERE n < 3
)
SELECT n FROM N
ORDER BY n;
Review source

column2: SQL Server limits a recursive CTE to {{c1::100 recursion levels}} by default.
column3:
This is a depth limit rather than a limit on the total result rows. One level can produce many rows.
Review source

column2: To limit a SQL Server recursive CTE to 200 recursion levels, use OPTION ({{c1::MAXRECURSION 200}}).
column3:
Use the hint when you know a valid hierarchy can exceed the default. It still protects against unexpectedly deep traversal.
WITH N AS (
    SELECT 1 AS n
    UNION ALL
    SELECT n + 1 FROM N WHERE n < 3
)
SELECT n FROM N
ORDER BY n
OPTION (MAXRECURSION 200);
Review source

column2: In SQL Server, OPTION (MAXRECURSION {{c1::0}}) removes the recursion limit.
column3:
Zero removes the safeguard. It does not cause the query to stop after the anchor.
WITH N AS (
    SELECT 1 AS n
    UNION ALL
    SELECT n + 1 FROM N WHERE n < 3
)
SELECT n FROM N
ORDER BY n
OPTION (MAXRECURSION 0);
Review source

column2: In a SQL Server SELECT using a recursive CTE, place OPTION (MAXRECURSION n) on {{c1::the outermost SELECT statement}}.
column3:
Set the limit on the statement using the CTE, not inside the parenthesized query.
WITH N AS (
    SELECT 1 AS n
    UNION ALL
    SELECT n + 1 FROM N WHERE n < 3
)
SELECT n FROM N
ORDER BY n
OPTION (MAXRECURSION 200);
Review source

column2: A recursive date CTE advances DateValue by one day with {{c1::DATEADD(DAY, 1, DateValue)}}.
column3:
The expression advances from one generated date to the next. The recursive filter decides when to stop generating.
WITH Dates AS (
    SELECT CAST('2025-01-01' AS date) AS DateValue
    UNION ALL
    SELECT DATEADD(DAY, 1, DateValue)
    FROM Dates WHERE DateValue < '2025-01-03'
)
SELECT DateValue FROM Dates;
Review source

column2: To retain generated CTE dates without matching orders, put the dates on the left of a {{c1::LEFT JOIN}}.
column3:
The join preserves a date even if none of the order rows satisfy the join condition.
WITH Dates AS (SELECT CAST('2025-01-01' AS date) AS DateValue)
SELECT d.DateValue, o.OrderID
FROM Dates AS d
LEFT JOIN dbo.Orders AS o ON o.OrderDate = d.DateValue;
Review source

column2: A CTE used by an UPDATE can define {{c1::the target rows to change}}.
column3:
The CTE expresses the row filter separately from the write. The UPDATE still changes the underlying table.
WITH Pending AS (
    SELECT Status FROM dbo.Orders WHERE Status = 'Pending'
)
UPDATE Pending SET Status = 'Ready';
Review source
